claims.text: A refractory high-entropy alloy powder mixture can comprise Nb, Mo, Ta, W, and Ti.
TiH2 or other hydride precursors facilitate hydrogen-mediated extrusion of these alloys.
The initial oxygen content should be below 500 ppm.
Pre-annealing hydride precursors at 400–600 °C removes loosely bound hydrogen and stabilizes the lattice.
Extrusion under ultra-high vacuum below 10^-6 Pa prevents oxygen uptake.
Hydride decomposition at 700–900 °C releases hydrogen gradually without rapid volume expansion or oxygen ingress.
Post-extrusion HIP at 1100–1200 °C and 100–150 MPa for 2–4 hours achieves full densification.
An extrusion strain rate of 0.01–0.1 s^-1 is required for the proposed process.
Released hydrogen acts as a transient lattice stabilizer that suppresses nucleation of alpha-HCP phases and TiO precipitates.
Oxygen introduced during refractory-alloy powder processing can produce TiO precipitates in a BCC matrix.
Oxygen uptake produces brittle alpha-HCP phases in Group IV-containing refractory high-entropy alloys.
TiO precipitates are brittle and promote embrittlement.
Gradually released hydrogen creates a reducing atmosphere inside the compact that prevents oxygen uptake.
Hydrogen mediation improves grain-boundary cohesion and dislocation mobility, thereby reducing catastrophic cracking during extrusion.
HIP preserves a metastable BCC solid solution that is critical for high-temperature yield strength.
The proposed route will produce a crack-free bulk alloy with at least 99.5% relative density.
The proposed route will produce a refined BCC microstructure with minimal alpha-HCP and TiO phases.
The resulting alloy will have a yield strength above 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and outperform conventionally processed alloys.
Conventional powder processing of Group IV-containing refractory high-entropy alloys can yield brittle or cracked products, while low-oxygen powder gives more promising results.
Keeping processing below 1200 °C avoids excessive grain growth or phase instability.
